description: We are a creative team participating in the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge. We want to transform satellite radar data into simple and engaging visualizations that help people understand Earth observation. Our project combines space science, coding, data analysis, design and storytelling. We welcome curious and motivated participants who want to collaborate and learn together.
summary:
Dancing with the SARs is an interactive Earth-observation forensic game that teaches users how to interpret NASA NISAR radar data. Players investigate nine missions involving calibration targets, floods, wildfires, earthquakes, data integrity, phishing, cloud security, telemetry intrusion, and web integrity.

The project transforms complex SAR evidence into guided investigations using interactive maps, radar measurements, before-and-after comparisons, coherence analysis, phase interpretation, hints, and verification flags. Each mission explains the scientific concept, guides the player through the analysis, and unlocks the next challenge after the correct solution is submitted.

This project makes satellite radar data more accessible to students and non-specialists while demonstrating how NASA Earth-observation data can support environmental monitoring, disaster analysis, and scientific investigation.
details:
Dancing with the SARs is an interactive Earth-observation and cybersecurity training platform built as a progressive Jeopardy-style forensic game. The player acts as a SAR analyst who investigates mission incidents using satellite imagery, radar measurements, metadata, image comparisons, logs, emails, access policies, and integrity reports.

All levels use the same NISAR/SAR-based Earth-observation framework and the same forensic analysis approach. However, each level uses different evidence and teaches a different concept. Depending on the mission, the evidence may include radar images, backscatter values, coherence measurements, interferometric fringes, weather information, satellite metadata, checksums, emails, authentication logs, cloud permissions, and website snapshots.

The project combines real NISAR radar previews with synthetic educational scenarios. Real NISAR L-band GCOV scenes are used for the Valencia and Merja Zerga investigations. The other missions use controlled synthetic evidence designed for training. These scenarios do not represent real emergencies or real cyberattacks.

The SAR data workflow preserves the original HDF5 files as source data and creates web-readable GeoTIFF and PNG products. The processing workflow removes NoData pixels, converts linear radar measurements to decibels when necessary, crops scenes to their common geographic intersection, aligns them to a common pixel grid, clips extreme values, and applies robust 2–98 percentile normalization. A median 5×5 speckle filter is used for the prepared visual products. The system also validates whether two scenes are comparable by checking their track, frame, pass direction, frequency, polarization, and measurement layer.

For the Valencia mission, the project compares two real NISAR HH scenes and generates before, after, change, and water-analysis layers. Because the scenes have different viewing geometries, the platform clearly treats this comparison as visual false-alarm training rather than a validated quantitative change-detection product. The airport runway appears dark because it is a smooth artificial surface, and the weather context does not support a major flood event.

For the Merja Zerga mission, the project uses two real NISAR scenes with compatible geometry. It applies Multi-Otsu classification to separate open water, wet surfaces, and land, then compares the two dates. The results show that rainfall increased the radar response of wet soil while the lagoon’s open-water core remained visible.

The remaining missions use a procedural SAR and forensic simulation engine. The system models radar backscatter, coherence, displacement, fringe count, geographic proximity, and surface classification. Level 0 teaches radar calibration using a trihedral reflector. Level 1 teaches how to distinguish a radar-dark runway from floodwater. Level 2 examines wildfire-related canopy decorrelation. Level 3 explains InSAR fringes and ground displacement. Level 4 teaches checksum, metadata, and timeline analysis. Level 5 teaches phishing and email forensics. Level 6 teaches cloud permissions and least-privilege security. Level 7 teaches telemetry-log correlation and intrusion reconstruction. Level 8 teaches website snapshot comparison, hashing, and web-asset integrity verification.

The game uses progressive unlocking. Level 0 is available first, and each following level becomes available only after the previous mission is solved. Players can click the map to sample coordinates, inspect SAR evidence, select the physical driver and recovery action, request hints, submit a verification flag, receive a score, and read a detailed explanation after completing a level.

Completion pop-ups explain the objective, the scientific concept, the investigation steps, the evidence, the result, and the skills learned. This helps beginners understand not only the answer, but also why the answer is scientifically and forensically correct.

The platform includes a mission welcome screen, a responsive SOC-style dashboard, an interactive geospatial map, before-and-after image comparison, SAR overlays, metadata panels, hints with scoring penalties, a leaderboard, session persistence, theme switching, reset functionality, generated player callsigns, and browser-based sound effects.

The project also includes a Gemini forensic assistant. The assistant analyzes only public challenge evidence and explains SAR signatures in clear English without revealing flags. The Gemini API key is kept on the server and is never exposed to the browser. The assistant is instructed to acknowledge when the evidence is insufficient.

The application was developed with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, server-side API routes, local JSON mission data, procedural SVG overlays, and the browser Web Audio API. Ground-truth flags are stored on the server and sanitized before challenge data is sent to the browser. Flag submissions use server-side verification, progressive unlock checks, hint penalties, spatial scoring, and rate limiting to reduce brute-force attempts.

The project’s main goal is to make complex SAR concepts understandable through an interactive investigation experience. It connects Earth science, disaster interpretation, cybersecurity, and data integrity. It teaches users that a radar signal must be interpreted using geometry, polarization, coherence, weather, metadata, and context rather than by relying on a single image or threshold.
